problem: An organization of 5 people can survive assigning permissions to individuals one at a time. An organization of 500 or 5,000 cannot — the moment headcount and folder/system count both grow, individual-by-individual permission assignment becomes an unmanageable, error-prone mess that nobody can audit or reason about.
Without groups, businesses run into problems that scale directly with headcount:
A new hire on the Finance team needs access to 15 different folders and 4 systems, and provisioning them one permission at a time takes hours and inevitably misses something.
When Finance gets a new shared drive, IT has to remember to individually add all 40 Finance employees rather than adding one group.
An audit asks "who can access payroll data" and the honest answer requires manually checking permissions across dozens of systems, because access was never tied to a consistent group structure.
An employee moves from Support to Engineering, and their old Support-only access is never removed because there was no single group membership to simply drop.
Two different admins independently grant the same person overlapping, inconsistent access because there's no single source of truth for "what should a person in this role have."

A group is the mechanism that turns permission management from an O(users × resources) problem into an O(groups) problem — instead of thinking about individuals, an organization thinks about roles, and lets group membership do the multiplication automatically.
concept: A group is a named collection of user accounts (and sometimes other groups) that can be granted permissions as a single unit. Rather than assigning a permission to each of 40 Finance employees individually, an admin assigns the permission once to a "Finance" group, and every current and future member of that group inherits it automatically.
Groups generally serve two distinct purposes, and enterprise environments usually keep them deliberately separate:
Security groups — used purely to grant or deny access to a resource (a file share, an application, a VPN profile).
Distribution/mailing groups — used purely to route communication (an email alias like support@company.com), with no access-control function at all.

A simple mental model: if a user account is an employee badge, a group is a lanyard color. Instead of the security desk checking each individual badge against a giant list of names, they just check "is this a blue lanyard" — and the building's doors are configured once, per lanyard color, rather than once per employee.
deep: 3.1 Linux/Unix groups Every Linux user has exactly one primary group (recorded directly in /etc/passwd) and can additionally belong to any number of secondary/supplementary groups (recorded in /etc/group). When a user creates a new file, it's normally owned by their primary group by default, unless the parent directory has the SGID bit set (Session 20), in which case the file inherits the directory's group instead.

File Purpose /etc/group Defines each group: name, GID, and list of member usernames /etc/gshadow Stores group password hashes (rarely used) and group administrators /etc/passwd Each user's line specifies their primary GID (not name — the numeric ID) Key commands: groupadd (create), groupdel (remove), usermod -aG groupname user (add a user to a supplementary group — the -a is critical, since omitting it replaces all existing supplementary groups instead of adding one), gpasswd (manage group membership and group administrators).

3.2 Windows groups Windows distinguishes group type (what the group is for) from group scope (how far the group can be used across a domain) — a distinction that trips up almost everyone learning Active Directory for the first time.

Group Scope Can Contain Members From Can Be Used On Domain Local Any domain in the forest (or trusted domains) Resources only within its own domain Global Only its own domain Resources in any domain in the forest (or trusted domains) Universal Any domain in the forest Resources anywhere in the forest Microsoft's long-standing best-practice pattern for this is often summarized as "A-G-DL-P": put user Accounts into Global groups, put Global groups into Domain Local groups, and assign Permissions to the Domain Local group. This layered structure keeps role definitions (Global groups) separate from resource access grants (Domain Local groups), which is exactly what makes large AD environments maintainable over years of organizational change.

3.3 Nested groups Both Linux and Windows allow groups to contain other groups, not just individual users. Nesting is powerful — a "Support-Managers" group can be nested inside a broader "Support-All" group so managers automatically get everything regular agents get, plus their own extra group's additional access.

But nesting also compounds risk: a permission granted to a group three levels up a nesting chain can grant access nobody reviewing the immediate group membership would ever notice, which is why nested-group sprawl is a recurring audit finding.

3.4 Effective permissions from multiple groups When a user belongs to several groups with different permissions on the same resource, the effective result generally follows an additive model (the union of all Allow rights across every group) except where an explicit Deny exists anywhere in the chain, in which case Deny wins regardless of how many Allow grants exist elsewhere (directly following the NTFS evaluation rule from Session 20).
workflow: Groups appear constantly in day-to-day identity and access operations:

Role-based provisioning: onboarding a new hire by adding them to a small, well-defined set of role- based groups (e.g., "Support-Agents", "VPN-Users", "All-Staff-Email") rather than granting individual permissions.

Resource access requests: creating a new Domain Local (or equivalent) group specifically scoped to a new shared folder or application, and granting access to that group rather than the requesting individual.
Group membership reviews: periodic audits of who belongs to sensitive groups (Domain Admins, Finance-Full-Access) — usually the single highest-priority item in any access-governance audit.
Role changes: removing a departing-role's group membership and adding the new role's group when someone transfers internally, directly preventing permission creep.

Naming convention governance: maintaining a consistent, documented group-naming scheme (e.g., prefix by type: SEC- for security groups, DL- for distribution lists) so a large directory stays navigable as it grows into hundreds of groups.
Group ownership assignment: designating a business owner (not just IT) responsible for approving membership changes to a given group, especially for self-service group management tools.
enterprise: Groups sit directly between Users (Session 21) and Permissions (Session 20) in Layer 2, acting as the connective layer that makes both scale. In Active Directory (Layer 4), groups are one of the most heavily used object types in the entire directory, and Group Policy (Session 60) itself is frequently scoped to security groups rather than applied blindly to entire Organizational Units.

In a mature enterprise, groups are usually the actual unit of access governance — compliance frameworks like SOX, ISO 27001, and PCI-DSS explicitly require documented, reviewable access controls, and in practice that review almost always happens at the group-membership level, not the individual-permission level, because that's the only level that stays humanly auditable at scale.

6. Dependencies (what Groups rely on) Depends On Why Users (Session 21) A group is fundamentally a container for user accounts (and other groups) — it has no meaning without underlying identities to hold.
Permissions (Session 20) Groups only matter because permissions can be assigned to them; a group with no permissions attached anywhere is functionally inert.
File Systems (Session 19) Group membership and group-based ACLs are ultimately stored and enforced using the same file-system metadata structures covered earlier.
Kernel (Session 12) The kernel resolves a process's full set of group memberships (the supplementary group list) as part of every access-check decision, not just its primary UID.
Directory Services / Active Directory (Session 51-52) At enterprise scale, group definitions and memberships are centrally stored and replicated by the directory service rather than kept per-machine.

7. Dependents (what relies on Groups) Depends on Groups Why Group Policy (Session 60) GPOs are commonly filtered to apply only to specific security groups rather than every object in an OU, making targeted policy delivery possible.
File Servers / Shares (Session 70) Enterprise file share access is almost always granted via groups rather than individual accounts, exactly as described throughout this session.

Least Privilege / Zero Trust (Sessions 85, 87) These security principles are only operationally achievable when access can be reasoned about and reviewed at the group level, not one account at a time.
Identity Governance (Session 66) Access certification/recertification campaigns are structured around reviewing group membership as the fundamental unit of "who has access to what."

Applications / Application Servers (Session 72) Many enterprise applications integrate with directory groups directly for role-based access within the app itself (e.g., an "App-Admins" AD group mapped to admin rights inside a ticketing system).
Incident Response (Session 100) Investigating a compromised account's potential blast radius requires enumerating every group it belonged to, since that's what actually defines what it could reach.
security: Privileged group membership is the highest-value target for attackers: compromising any account that's a member of Domain Admins (or local Administrators, or root-equivalent groups) is frequently the actual end goal of a lateral-movement attack, not just a means to an end.

Nested-group blast radius: as described in 3.3, deeply nested groups can silently grant access several hops away from what a quick membership check would reveal — attackers who understand this structure specifically hunt for these indirect paths (this is the core idea behind attack-path tools like BloodHound).

Group Scope confusion (Windows): assigning permissions directly to a Global or Universal group instead of following the A-G-DL-P pattern makes future auditing and permission changes far harder to track cleanly across a growing forest.

Self-service group sprawl: allowing broad self-service group creation without governance leads to hundreds of poorly-named, overlapping, undocumented groups that no one can confidently clean up later.

Dynamic/rule-based groups: modern directories (Azure AD dynamic groups) can auto-populate membership from user attributes (department, job title) — powerful for consistency, but a misconfigured rule can silently and rapidly grant broad access to the wrong population.

Empty or unused groups: groups that still hold permissions but have had all their members removed over time are a common overlooked cleanup gap, sometimes rediscovered and repopulated incorrectly years later.

Separation of duties: certain group combinations (e.g., someone who can both create purchase orders AND approve them) represent a security/fraud risk regardless of whether each individual permission looks reasonable alone — this is why access reviews look at combinations of group membership, not just single groups in isolation.
troubleshooting: Symptom Likely Cause First Diagnostic Step User added to group still lacks access Kerberos ticket/access token not refreshed since the group change Have the user log off/on (or klist purge on Windows) to force a new token containing the updated group SIDs User has access they shouldn't after a role change Old role's group membership was never removed, only the new one added Review full group membership list, not just the groups relevant to their current role Linux user in a group per /etc/group still gets Permission Denied Group added without -a flag on usermod, overwriting other supplementary groups, or session predates the change Run `groups username` and compare to `id username`; have the user start a new login session Nested group doesn't seem to inherit expected permissions Group nesting depth or type exceeds what the target system/OS actually supports or evaluates Check platform-specific nesting limits (e.g., some applications only read direct membership, not nested) Access review can't determine why a user has access Access was granted through a deeply nested or indirect group chain rather than direct, documented membership Use a group membership/effective- access reporting tool rather than manually walking nested groups by hand Dynamic group membership shows unexpected members Attribute-based rule is broader or differently scoped than intended Review the exact rule logic and test against a sample of accounts before trusting the full population
example: A support/CEx organization (comparable to a FundedNext-style operations environment) initially manages file-share access by adding individual employees directly to NTFS ACLs, one name at a time, because the team was small and it felt simpler than "setting up groups for just a few people."

As the team grows past 60 agents across multiple shifts and specializations (KYC review, refunds, ethics escalations), this approach collapses under its own weight: no one can quickly answer who has access to the ethics escalation folder, removing a departing agent means manually finding and removing their name from a dozen different ACLs across different shares, and two different team leads have each independently granted slightly different sets of permissions to agents with the same job title.

The remediation is a direct application of this session's core idea: IT creates role-based security groups (Support-Agents, Support-KYC, Support-Ethics-Reviewers, Support-Leads), maps each existing share's ACL to the appropriate group instead of individual names, and moves every current employee into the correct group based on their actual role. Onboarding a new agent now takes one group addition instead of a dozen individual ACL edits, and answering "who can see ethics escalations" becomes a single membership query instead of a multi-day investigation.
cloud: Azure AD/Entra ID groups extend the same security-group concept to cloud resources and SaaS applications, and additionally support dynamic membership rules based on user or device attributes, reducing manual membership management at scale.

AWS IAM groups let permission policies be attached once to a group and inherited by every IAM user added to it — directly mirroring the on-prem A-G-DL-P philosophy, though AWS increasingly favors roles and permission sets (via IAM Identity Center) over static IAM users and groups for many use cases.
Google Cloud IAM groups (via Google Groups) work similarly, allowing a single group to be granted a role across one or many GCP projects at once.

Cloud environments often introduce a hybrid pattern: on-prem AD groups synced to the cloud directory (Azure AD Connect) so an organization can keep a single authoritative group structure that governs both on-prem file shares and cloud application access simultaneously.
automation: Role-based provisioning scripts: HR-triggered automation that adds a new hire to a predefined bundle of groups matching their job title, rather than an admin manually selecting groups from memory.
PowerShell (Add-ADGroupMember, Get-ADGroupMember, Get-ADPrincipalGroupMembership) is the standard toolkit for bulk group operations and auditing effective group membership across an AD forest.

Configuration management (Ansible's `group` module, Puppet's `group` resource) enforces consistent local group existence and membership across large Linux server fleets, keeping drift from accumulating machine by machine.

Automated stale-group and empty-group reports: scheduled scripts that flag groups with zero members, groups that haven't changed membership in years, or groups nested more than a defined depth, feeding directly into periodic cleanup work.

Access certification tooling (Identity Governance platforms) automates the recurring "does this person still need this group" review cycle described in Section 4, replacing manual spreadsheet- based audits.
career: Group design and management is one of the clearest signals of IT maturity in a candidate — anyone can add a user to a folder's ACL, but understanding role-based group structure separates support-level thinking from sysadmin/architect-level thinking.

Help Desk / Support: handling day-to-day "add me to this group" and "why don't I have access" tickets, and learning to recognize when a request actually calls for a new group rather than another individual grant.
Systems Administrator: designing the group taxonomy and naming convention an entire organization's access model will run on for years.
IAM / Identity Governance Specialist: owning access certification campaigns and group-based least- privilege enforcement at an enterprise scale.
Security Analyst: mapping attack paths through nested-group privilege chains, a skill directly used in tools like BloodHound and in real incident response.
Cloud Architect: designing hybrid group-sync strategies and IAM group/role structures that stay maintainable as an organization's cloud footprint grows.

For someone building from a support foundation, recognizing "this is a groups problem, not an individual-permissions problem" is exactly the kind of judgment that marks the transition from ticket- taker to infrastructure designer.

4. A user was just added to a group but still can't access the resource — what's your troubleshooting process?
5. Why can nested groups be a security risk even when each individual group's permissions look reasonable?
6. How would you design a group structure from scratch for a support organization with agents, leads, and specialized review teams?

misconceptions: "Adding someone to a group grants access instantly, everywhere, immediately." — Existing sessions/tickets (Kerberos, cached tokens) often don't reflect the change until the user logs off and back on, which is a constant source of "but I already added them!" confusion.

"More groups always means more organization and control." — Uncontrolled group sprawl, especially from unrestricted self-service creation, produces the opposite: an unauditable maze that's harder to reason about than a smaller, well-governed set.

"A user's direct group memberships tell you their full effective access." — Nested groups mean real effective access can extend several hops beyond what's directly visible without specialized tooling to trace the full chain.

"Removing someone from a group is just as safe/reversible as adding them." — It is generally safe and is in fact the correct way to walk back access, but removal timing matters just as much as addition timing during role changes and offboarding.

"Distribution groups can't cause a security problem since they're just for email." — A distribution group can still leak sensitive information broadly if membership is wrong, and in many directories a distribution group can be converted to a mail-enabled security group, so scope and purpose should never be assumed from the name alone.

"Group scope in Active Directory is just a technical detail that doesn't matter much." — Choosing the wrong scope (e.g., assigning permissions directly to a Global group instead of following A-G- DL-P) is a common root cause of unmaintainable, hard-to-migrate access structures years later.
anchors: Group = lanyard color; the security desk checks the lanyard, not each individual badge, and doors are configured once per color, not once per person.
A-G-DL-P = Accounts wear a Global lanyard for their role, and that lanyard gets clipped onto a Domain Local keyring that actually opens the door — Permissions live on the keyring, not the lanyard.
Nested groups = Russian nesting dolls of access — opening the outer doll doesn't tell you everything hidden inside the smaller ones without actually checking each layer.
Distribution group vs. security group = a mailing list sign-up sheet versus a building keycard — one routes messages, the other opens doors, and confusing the two is a real risk.
Stale group membership = an old lanyard nobody collected when someone changed teams — still opens doors it shouldn't, silently, until someone actually checks.
Dynamic group = a self-updating guest list that reads everyone's job title from a spreadsheet and re- issues lanyards automatically — powerful, but only as safe as the rule that drives it.
connections: Session 12 (Kernel): the kernel resolves a process's complete supplementary group list on every access check, not just its primary group — groups are enforced at exactly the same fundamental level as individual permissions.
Session 17 (Services): service accounts are sometimes added to dedicated groups to scope exactly what a service can touch, rather than granting broad individual permissions directly to the account.

Session 19 (File Systems) & Session 20 (Permissions): group-based ACLs are stored using the same file-system metadata structures already covered, and everything about Deny/Allow evaluation order from Session 20 applies identically whether the ACE names a user or a group.

Session 21 (Users): this session is the direct continuation of that one — users are the individual identities; groups are how those identities get organized and managed at scale, which is precisely the gap Session 21 left open.

Session 18 (Logging): audit logs frequently need to record not just which user performed an action but which group-derived permission actually authorized it, which matters heavily during incident investigation.

This session completes the core Layer 2 identity/access trio (Permissions → Users → Groups) and is the direct technical foundation for Active Directory (52), Group Policy (60), and Identity Governance (66) later in Layer 4 — none of those systems can be properly understood without first internalizing how group-based access actually resolves.

18. Diagrams (Described) Diagram A — Individual permissions vs. group-based permissions at scale [Without groups: 40 employees × 15 folders = 600 individual permission assignments to create, track, and eventually remove] versus [With groups: 40 employees added to 1 group, that group assigned to 15 folders = 40 group memberships + 15 group-to-folder grants = 55 total relationships to manage]. The larger the organization, the more dramatic this gap becomes.

Diagram B — A-G-DL-P nesting pattern [User Accounts] → placed into → [Global Group, representing a role, e.g., 'Finance-Analysts'] → nested into → [Domain Local Group, representing a resource grant, e.g., 'DL-FinanceShare-Modify'] → which is directly assigned → [NTFS Permission on the actual folder]. Role definition and resource access are deliberately kept in separate group layers.

Diagram C — Effective access resolution across multiple groups [User is a member of Group A (Allow: Read) + Group B (Allow: Write) + Group C (Deny: Delete)] → [System collects all ACEs from all group SIDs the user holds] → [Result: Read + Write granted (union of Allows), Delete blocked (explicit Deny overrides any Allow anywhere in the chain)].
lab: Hands-on exercises to build real muscle memory. Use a disposable VM or test machine.
Linux 9. Create a group with groupadd project-team, then add two existing test users to it using usermod -aG project-team username — verify with `groups username` for each.
10.Create a shared directory owned by the project-team group with the SGID bit set, have both users create a file inside it, and confirm both files inherit the group automatically.

11.Deliberately run usermod -G (without -a) on one of the test users to add them to a new group, then check `groups username` again and observe what happened to their other supplementary group memberships — explain why this is a common mistake.
12.Remove a user from the group with gpasswd -d username project-team and confirm the change with `id username` after starting a fresh session.

Windows (or AD lab environment if available) 13.Create a Global security group representing a role and a Domain Local security group representing a resource grant, nest the Global group inside the Domain Local group, and assign the Domain Local group Modify rights on a test folder — confirm a test user in the Global group gets the expected access.

14.Use PowerShell's Get-ADPrincipalGroupMembership on a test user to list every group they belong to, including nested ones, and compare that to what a quick glance at the user's direct "Member Of" tab shows.

15.Create a dynamic/rule-based group (or simulate the logic on paper if no Azure AD tenant is available) based on a department attribute, and identify one edge case where the rule could unintentionally include or exclude the wrong people.

Reflection After the lab, write one paragraph explaining, in your own words, why the A-G-DL-P pattern separates "who someone is" (role) from "what a resource allows" (grant), and what breaks down in a large organization if that separation isn't maintained.
